title: Your first five minutes in a medical emergency
summary: For anyone who has never done first aid: check the scene, talk to the dispatcher, then CPR, severe bleeding, choking and the recovery position, ending with how to practise.

steps.title: Check the scene, then check the person, before you act
steps.body: Before you touch anyone, look for danger to you: traffic, fire, live wires, an unstable crash. Then tap their shoulder, shout their name, and look at their chest for no more than ten seconds. No response and no normal breathing means you need help now.
steps.deeper:
A hurt rescuer helps no one, so a two-second look around keeps you useful. The ten-second breathing check is short on purpose: the American Heart Association teaches that gasping is not normal breathing, and a long search for a pulse only delays the help they need.

Imagine someone slumped at the wheel of a car at a roadside. You park well back, switch your hazard lights on, walk up, tap the window and shout. They do not answer and their chest does not rise. Now you know this is an emergency, and you act.

Apply it today: next time you enter a room or street scene, practise saying out loud, 'safe, shout, shake, breathing'. Then book a hands-on first aid class with the American Red Cross or the American Heart Association to rehearse it on a manikin.

steps.title: Stay on the line, because the dispatcher is part of your team
steps.body: Call 911 (999 or 112 in many countries), put the phone on speaker and leave it next to you. Give the exact location first, then say what happened and how many people are hurt. Answer the questions, and do not hang up until the dispatcher says you can.
steps.deeper:
Dispatchers are trained to guide callers through the first minutes. They can tell you how to do compressions, count with you, and warn you when conditions change. Hanging up early removes that coach, and the ambulance is usually already on its way while they ask questions.

Say a friend collapses at a barbecue. You say, 'I am at 14 Elm Street, behind the white garage. My friend collapsed and is not breathing.' The dispatcher asks if they are awake, then talks you into starting CPR while someone else unlocks the gate for the ambulance.

Apply it today: learn your exact address or the way to describe where you are, and make sure everyone at home can say it too. Then join an American Red Cross or American Heart Association class, where instructors rehearse real call scenarios with you.

steps.title: Push in the centre of the chest, deep, fast, and let it rise
steps.body: Kneel beside them, put the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, and the other hand on top. Lock your elbows and push straight down about 2 inches (5 to 6 cm), at 100 to 120 compressions a minute. Let the chest rise fully each time.
steps.deeper:
Compressions squeeze the heart between breastbone and spine to push blood to the brain. Full recoil lets the heart refill before the next push, and pauses stop blood flow, so keep interruptions as short as you can. The American Heart Association points to a steady beat of 100 to 120 a minute.

Many people use the tempo of a familiar song with that pace to keep rhythm. Trade places with another rescuer every two minutes if there is one, because tired compressions get shallow, and keep going until help arrives or an AED tells you what to do.

Apply it today: tap out 100 to 120 beats a minute with a song you know, then practise on a cushion to feel the depth. Finish by enrolling in a hands-on CPR class with the American Heart Association or American Red Cross, where a manikin shows you real depth and recoil.

steps.title: When pressure fails on a limb, a tourniquet can save a life
steps.body: Call 911 first. If blood from an arm or leg soaks through and pressure is not controlling it, put a tourniquet on, about 2 inches above the wound and never on a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops, and note the time.
steps.deeper:
Heavy limb bleeding can be fatal in minutes, and hands can tire or slip. A tourniquet squeezes the main vessel shut, so it is a tool for severe, life-threatening bleeding that pressure is not stopping. Stop the Bleed training teaches that it will hurt, and that this is expected when it is tight enough.

Imagine a deep cut to a thigh from a chainsaw accident. A bystander calls for help, then applies a commercial tourniquet above the wound and turns the rod until the bleeding stops. They write the time on it and leave it on for the paramedics.

Apply it today: find out where the nearest bleeding control kit is at your work or gym. Then take a Stop the Bleed course, or an American Red Cross class, to practise applying a real tourniquet with an instructor watching.

source.title: Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons)

steps.title: For a choking adult, alternate five back blows and five thrusts
steps.body: If they cannot cough, speak or breathe, have someone call 911. Stand to the side and slightly behind, lean them forward, and give five firm back blows between the shoulder blades. Then give five abdominal thrusts, and repeat until the object comes out.
steps.deeper:
The Red Cross teaches this five-and-five pattern because each method can dislodge the object in a different way. For thrusts, wrap your arms around the waist, make a fist just above the navel, and pull sharply inward and upward. Stop once they breathe, cough, or speak, and have them seen by a doctor afterward.

Imagine a colleague grabs their throat at lunch and cannot make a sound. You shout for someone to call 911, lean them forward and give five back blows, then five thrusts. If they go limp, lower them to the floor and start CPR, checking the mouth for the object.

Apply it today: rehearse the hand positions on a willing friend without any force. Then sign up for an American Red Cross first aid class, where you can practise back blows and thrusts on a manikin.

steps.title: After you roll them to their side, keep watching their breathing
steps.body: Putting someone on their side does not end your job. Stay with them, keep the dispatcher on the line, and watch their chest and face. If they stop breathing normally, roll them onto their back, tell the dispatcher, and start CPR.
steps.deeper:
Someone who is unresponsive can get worse without warning, and the side position only keeps the airway clear. Your attention is what catches the change. This is the whole sequence in one line: check the scene, call and stay on the line, then CPR, bleeding control, or choking help as needed.

Picture a friend who passed out after a fall and is now breathing but not waking. You roll them, keep your phone on speaker, and count their breaths. After a few minutes the breathing goes quiet, so you roll them back and begin compressions as the dispatcher coaches.

Apply it today: run through the whole sequence out loud with a friend, from the scene check to the call to each step. Then book a hands-on class with the American Red Cross or the American Heart Association, because only practice makes the steps automatic.
